audio.t: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the first-year EMI orientation. I'm Doctor Huang, the coordinator of the English-Medium Instruction program. Starting next semester, about a third of your required courses will be taught in English. I know many of you feel nervous about that, so let me explain what support is available.

First, every EMI course has a teaching assistant who holds office hours twice a week. You can ask questions in English or in Mandarin. The goal is understanding, not perfect grammar. Second, most professors share their slides at least one day before class, so I strongly recommend previewing them and writing down any unfamiliar terms.

Finally, you won't be graded on your accent. Exams focus on subject knowledge, and in many courses you may use a bilingual dictionary during tests. If a course still feels too difficult after three weeks, talk to your advisor about switching to a Mandarin section, as long as one is offered. Any questions so far?

head: From: Professor Daniel Kao
To: Students in Introduction to Economics (EMI)
Subject: Changes to our class starting next week
passage:
Dear all,
Thank you for your hard work on the first quiz. Based on your feedback in the mid-semester survey, I am making a few adjustments to how our class runs.

Starting next Monday, I will speak more slowly and pause after each main section so that you can ask questions. I will also upload the slides by Sunday evening instead of on the morning of class. Several of you said the readings were too long, so I have shortened them and added a short video summary for each chapter.

Please note that the final project report must still be written in English. However, your group presentation may include up to five minutes of Chinese if you need to clarify a difficult concept. Feel free to come to my office hours on Wednesdays from 1 to 3 p.m. if you have any concerns.
Best,
Professor Kao

Because the class is moving to a new room

passage: Three years ago, only a handful of courses at our university were taught entirely in English. This semester, the number has risen to more than 120, part of a national plan to prepare students for international careers. But a new survey by the Student Association suggests that the rapid growth has left some students struggling.

Of the 850 students who responded, 62 percent said they understood "most" of what was said in their English-medium classes. However, nearly a third admitted that they often relied on classmates or translation apps to keep up, and 18 percent said they had avoided EMI courses altogether because they feared getting lower grades.

Professors see the issue from a different angle. "Many students understand more than they think," said Dr. Grace Lee, who teaches environmental science in English. "The real problem is confidence. They are afraid to speak up because they worry about making mistakes in front of their classmates." To address this, Dr. Lee lets students submit questions anonymously through the learning platform before each class.

The university has responded by expanding its support services. Starting next semester, every EMI course will be assigned a bilingual teaching assistant, and the Language Center will offer free weekly workshops on academic listening and presentation skills. The university is also considering a policy that would allow students to take one EMI course per semester on a pass/fail basis.

Not everyone is convinced. Some students argue that the courses should simply offer more explanations in Mandarin. Still, Student Association president Kevin Tsai believes the trend is positive. "Employers want graduates who can work in English," he said. "We just need the right support to get there."
